newsitem.title: MALTA: Ministers urge speeding up of Euro-Med spending.
newsitem.headline: Ministers urge speeding up of Euro-Med spending.

text.p: European Union and Mediterranean countries on Wednesday chided each other for the slow pace of a $6.3 billion partnership programme but pledged greater effort to boost trade and investment.
Officials gathered for a meeting of EU and 12 Mediterranean foreign ministers said it was clear the so-called "Barcelona Process" needed to be speeded up.
Launched in Spain in November 1995, the programme seeks to direct over $6 billion in European aid, soft loans and investment to the Mediterranean before the end of the century.
The ultimate goal is to turn region into a free-trade area by the year 2010.
"This economic and financial cooperation requires impetus," Tunisian Foreign Minister Abderrahim Zouari told the conference. "I suggest a special effort by senior officials to target this."
Turkey's Ufuk Soylemez, standing in for foreign minister Tansu Ciller, also criticised the slow pace of the process.
"The driving force ... must be trade and investment," he said. "Fiancial figures show that this is not the case."
Soylemez highlighted Turkey's own experience with the EU as an example of how treaties with the 15-nation bloc can frequently run into problems.
He said the full benefits of a Turkish customs union with the EU had yet to be realised ... "mainly due to reasons which have nothing to do with the agreement".
He was referring to Greece's blocking of promised financial packages to Turkey because of differences between Ankara and Athens over Cyprus and a series of rocky islets in the Agean Sea.
"Should this position continue, Turkey will inevitably reassess its position in the Euromed process," he said.
Portugal's Francisco Seixas da Costa, said Mediterranean partners had to take some of the blame for delays.
"Financial efforts in the north have perhaps not been what we might like, but regional integration in the south could also be better," he said.
Britain said it would press Mediterranean countries to accelerate economic and financial reforms when it takes over the EU presidency next year.

"It is clear that we must follow through this theme if the region is to start to receive a larger share of global investment flows," said Baroness Lynda Chalker, minister of state for overseas development.
Chalker said Britain was considering hosting a conference in 1998 to focus on financial market reform.

"I am pleased to announce that we shall continue work on this initiative," she said. "Deregulation, privatisation, financial sector reform and the development of capital markets all have the potential to play a crucial role in encouraging private sector investment."
